revisions.title: The image test
revisions.body: At 430e–431e, Socrates places a name beside a painted portrait: each is an imitation offered to a different sense. The comparison makes correctness a question of fit rather than a bare yes-or-no identity. As with a painting, a name may still be an image when elements are omitted or added; what changes is whether the rendering is fine or shoddy. Listen for the shift from asking whether a name imitates to asking how well it does so.

body: "Cratylus’s praise does not close the inquiry; it gives Socrates a reason to reopen it. Socrates first invites Cratylus to teach him, then turns that apparent deference into a test of the claim that every genuine name is correct: the name “Hermogenes” forces the question whether a misnaming is false speech or merely noise. From there, the name-as-image analogy shifts the standard from confidence to comparison. Read the unit as admiration converted into accountability."
